title: 「问一下又不会怎样？」——Dlala Studios 谈如何大胆出手，为即将推出的游戏 Murals 请到喜剧传奇 Bob Mortimer
content:
"What's the harm in asking?" – Dlala Studios on taking a big swing to get comedy legend Bob Mortimer for the upcoming game Murals | GamesIndustry.biz
If you click on a link and make a purchase we may receive a small commission.
Read our editorial policy
.
The name Bob Mortimer might not mean much to those who haven't lived in the UK, but he's a huge deal in the world of British comedy.
He's one of the country's top comedians, having starred in the double act Reeves and Mortimer, and he recently won the UK version of Amazon's Last One Laughing game show. He's also – as
revealed at Gamescom Opening Night Live 2026
– a voice performer in the upcoming game
Murals
from developer Dlala Studios.
Aj Grand-Scrutton  |
Image credit:
Dlala Studios
Mortimer's involvement began when company founder Aj Grand-Scrutton and lead writer Kelsy Abbott wrote a character that was a "rip-off" of the comedian. Then they wondered whether they could actually get the real thing.
"One day I was sitting at my desk, and thought: 'What's the harm in just asking?'," Grand-Scrutton tells
GamesIndustry.biz
at Gamescom. "So I rung up Mark [Landers] at
Side
, and I just said, 'Hey dude, is there any chance we could reach out to Bob Mortimer's people?' And he went, 'Oh yeah, hold on Aj mate, I'll get back to you'. And in a couple of hours he called me back, and he was like, we've found his agent and manager, they like the idea, they're interested. Bob wants to see a script."
All they had was a "bunch of gags" at that point, so Grand-Scrutton and Abbott stayed up all night writing a two-to-three-page script, then waited for Bob's verdict. The Dlala founder says it was "the longest 48 hours" of his life.
"I'm like, 'Oh my God, why did we think we could write Bob Mortimer-style comedy and show it to Bob Mortimer?'" he recalls. "Kelsy's losing her mind as well, she's like, 'How arrogant are we? We've just tried to be Bob to Bob.' And then they came back, and they were like: 'He loves it. He'd love to be a part of this'."
Murals features Bob Mortimer as 'Magic Dave'  |
Image credit:
Dlala Studios
Later down the line, Grand-Scrutton was in London for a recording session with Mortimer – Dlala always directs its voiceover work.
"I'm not going to say we directed him, because he didn't need it: Everything that came out of his mouth was perfect," the studio founder laughs. "Honestly, the Bob Mortimer you see on television, he's even a hundred times nicer and funnier than that in person."
Earned trust
Securing a celebrity of Mortimer's calibre is a far cry from Dlala's rather humble roots. Founded in 2012 by Grand-Scrutton and Craig Thomas – who had met at
Jagex
– the outfit initially operated out of Grand-Scrutton's garage in Witham, Essex. Now the company is 43 staff strong and is based in an office around the corner from where Grand-Scrutton grew up.
Dlala made the 2020 game Battletoads  |
Image credit:
Dlala Studios/Xbox Game Studios/Rare
Since those early days, the studio has made a name for itself working on other companies' IP. In 2020, the company released Battletoads, based on the iconic Rare franchise, before
launching Disney Illusion Island three years later
.
"Obviously Battletoads and Illusion Island were these two great IPs, but we've never done a traditional license deal," Grand-Scrutton says. "We have always been directly contracted or recruited by the IP holders."
The Battletoads deal came about after a period where Dlala was doing work-for-hire; one project the company was working on was Sea of Thieves. A combination of earned trust and persistence helped the studio land the IP.
"With Battletoads, Microsoft let Rare have a lot of autonomy with that IP back in the day," Grand-Scrutton explains. "We helped out on Sea of Thieves. Dlala was about 12 people at the time, and for the six months before Sea of Thieves came out, the whole of Dlala was helping Rare get that finished. And I think that earned trust.
"I met [former Rare studio head]
Craig Duncan
in the year we formed, 2012, and every year, I sent him multiple pitches for Battletoads, trying to wear him down. It wasn't until 2016 that he said we should do this, and we still didn't get it over the line until 2018. That was a real kismet of stuff; we proved ourselves with Sea of Thieves and Game Pass needed portfolio pieces. And once that came out, it showed the quality of what we could do and deliver end to end."
Disney's Illusion Island came out in 2023  |
Image credit:
Dlala Studios/Disney
That, in turn, led to a deal with Disney for Illusion Island – which marked Dlala's second deal with the firm, after an initial project didn't work out. "I did
a rather honest GI.biz interview
that I shouldn't have done, where I mentioned we had a Disney game in 2015 that got cancelled in 2016, and I thought we'd never work with them ever again," recalls Grand-Scrutton.
"It was kind of like high school boyfriend and girlfriend meeting up after 20 years"
"After Battletoads came out, we were looking at what we could do next, and I said as a joke: 'Oh, why don't we give Disney a call?' and we all went 'Oh ha ha'. Then we all went: 'Oh, why
don't
we give Disney a call?' So we spoke. It was kind of like high school boyfriend and girlfriend meeting up after 20 years: this is how I've changed, this is how you've changed. And we said on that call: 'Should we give it another go? Should we try and do a game together?'"
Grand-Scrutton says when it comes to deal negotiations, Dlala isn't about making aggressive pitches with promises of giant profits. "Our pitch has always been like, we love this IP, and we could do something cool with it. Hopefully it's a success if we work together.'"
Going it alone
After securing those IP deals with Rare and Disney, you'd think that Dlala's next move might be another licensed property. But instead the studio has made a bet on making its own IP. "We were presented with a real opportunity where we had a little bit of money ourselves in the bank so we could a
